doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Johnny Mathis records and Hyman's whistling
summary: He identifies Chances Are and whistling on records, his Moritat hit, and joining AFTRA.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: So if you listened to — I don’t know if you ever sit and listen to the oldies station —
I do.
Are you likely to hear yourself?
Very much.
And do you remember —
Yeah, I remember some.
Can you tell me a couple of spots that I might hear?
Yeah. Johnny Mathis, there’s one — there’s a famous Mathis record that begins with a piano figure. “Chances Are.”
“Chances Are.” Yes. That’s you?
That’s one. Yeah. And then there’s another one that I whistled on for Johnny Mathis.
[whistles]
[hums].
That’s right. And there’s another Bob Allen song.
“Wonderful Wonderful.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
Right.
That’s you whistling is that right?

That was one of my — well you know I had made my own — I have to admit — hit record of “Moritat,” which then became known as “Theme from the Three Penny Opera” and then finally became known as “Mack the Knife” in 1955 for MGM as the Dick Hyman Trio which actually had four people in it I think. And I whistled on it as well as playing an instrument called the harpsichord piano. So it became known around town that I was willing and I was capable of whistling. Willing to undertake it and capable of doing it without running out of breath. So I found myself being called to be a whistler on dates and I promptly joined AFTRA, that is the singers union, because their scale was higher than the musician’s union, and on a good day I might collect both scales on a single session. So I’m the whistler on that and I’m the whistler on something with Nye and Marlowe for Archie Bleier’s company Cadence, something called “The Man in the Raincoat,” one of those spooky “Third Man” theme type recordings.
Was it a lip whistle or was it a teeth whistle?
No, no, no. The teeth whistling we left to Bob Haggart.
Oh, of course.
No, it was regular whistling. And I did a fair number of those things and they are very funny to think about now. After a while I dropped or suspended my membership in AFTRA.
